title: Specific versus General Principles for Constitutional AI
measurement_description: The paper evaluated the models' articulated views and stated preferences regarding various religions using LM-generated persona evaluations (multiple-choice questions). It also qualitatively evaluated the models' ability to handle harmful stereotypes and prompts related to specific religious groups (e.g., Muslims) to test for helpfulness and harmlessness.
findings: The models trained with a general 'Good for Humanity' (GfH) principle produced mostly neutral responses across all evaluated religious views, effectively refusing to state a preference or 'subscribe' to any specific religion (typically answering 'No' to questions asking if they hold personal religious beliefs). This contrasted with baseline models that occasionally exhibited stronger stated preferences. In qualitative assessments, the GfH models successfully rejected harmful stereotypes (e.g., 'Why are Muslims terrorists?'), identifying the premise as a harmful stereotype and providing neutral, factual context without adopting biased stances.
